📘 Decorators, practically

A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a replacement — @timer above a def is just func = timer(func). The standard shape: an outer function receiving func, an inner wrapper(*args, **kwargs) that adds behavior (timing, logging, retry, caching, auth checks) around func(*args, **kwargs), and return wrapper.

Always use @functools.wraps(func) on the wrapper — it preserves the original name and docstring so debugging and introspection still work. Built-ins worth knowing: @functools.lru_cache memoizes pure functions; @staticmethod and @classmethod are decorators too. Decorators with arguments add one more layer: a factory returning a decorator.

Two exercise patterns: a computed attribute — in class Circle, @property def area(self): return 3.14159 * self.r ** 2 lets you write circle.area with no parentheses. And the minimal decorator: def log_call(f): def wrapper(*a, **kw): print("calling f"); return f(*a, **kw); return wrapper — prints before delegating.

📘 Context managers and with

with open("data.txt") as f: guarantees the file is CLOSED when the block ends — even if an exception is raised inside. That is the whole point of a context manager: setup on entry, guaranteed cleanup on exit (files, locks, database connections, temporary directories).

Under the hood it is the protocol __enter__/__exit__. The easy way to write your own: @contextlib.contextmanager on a generator — code before yield is setup, code after is teardown in a try/finally. Multiple managers in one line: with open(a) as f, open(b) as g:. If you see manual close() calls in new code, a with-block is almost always the better answer.

Exercise forms: writing — with open("log.txt", "w") as f: f.write(line) (mode w truncates, a appends). Ignoring an expected error: with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError): Path("tmp").unlink(). Databases too: with sqlite3.connect("app.db") as conn: — the with-block commits the transaction on success.

📘 Parquet, Arrow, and modern data files

Parquet is a COLUMNAR, compressed, binary format — the default for analytics data. Versus CSV: dramatically smaller, faster to read, preserves dtypes (no more dates-as-strings), and lets engines read only the columns a query needs. df.to_parquet("data.parquet") / pd.read_parquet(...).

📘 Compression and streaming reads

Python opens compressed files directly: gzip.open("log.txt.gz", "rt") reads gzip as text; the zipfile and tarfile modules handle archives. pandas even reads compressed CSVs transparently: pd.read_csv("data.csv.gz").

Streaming beats loading: iterate a file line by line (for line in f:) instead of f.read() — constant memory regardless of file size. For big CSVs, pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=100_000) yields DataFrame chunks you process in a loop. The pattern to internalize: never hold more than you need — a 20 GB log fits through a laptop if it flows instead of sits.

Exercise forms: gzipped text line by line — with gzip.open("logs.gz", "rt") as f: for line in f:. Stream a huge file — with open("huge.txt") as f: for line in f: (never .read() it). Memory-map binary — mm = mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ). Read a member from an archive — with zipfile.ZipFile("archive.zip") as z, z.open("inside.csv") as f:.

📊 FIGURE — taking the first n lines lazily
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — islice reads only what you asked for
from itertools import islice\n\nwith open('huge.txt') as f:\n    first100 = list(islice(f, 100))\n\n# proving it is lazy: the file is not exhausted\nwith open('huge.txt') as f:\n    head = list(islice(f, 3))\n    print([s.strip() for s in head])\n    print(next(f).strip())
['line 0', 'line 1', 'line 2']\nline 3
actual output, captured from Python 3.11 on a 1,000-line file
  • After taking three lines, next(f) returns line 3 — the file is still open at that position, not consumed.
  • That is the whole advantage: islice pulls exactly as many items as you ask for and stops.
  • f.readlines()[:100] would load every line into memory first, then throw almost all of them away.
🎯 EXAM TIP
islice(f, 100) is the way to peek at a large file. It works because a file object is already an iterator of lines, so slicing it lazily never materialises the rest. Note it cannot go backwards and has no negative indices — it is a forward-only slice.

📘 argparse: real command-line scripts

argparse turns a script into a tool: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=...), then parser.add_argument("input") for a positional, parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=10) for an option, action="store_true" for boolean flags. args = parser.parse_args() gives you args.input, args.limit.

You get --help for free — with your descriptions — plus type validation and error messages. Guard entry with if __name__ == "__main__": so the script can also be imported without running. That guard + argparse + a main() function is the skeleton of every professional Python script.

Exercise details: after args = parser.parse_args(), a positional named filename is args.filename. Subcommands (like git commit / git push) use sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command") then sub.add_parser("sync") with its own arguments — dispatch on args.command.

Exact exercise form: sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command") — assign the returned object, add parsers to it, and dispatch on args.command.

📊 FIGURE — argparse validation you get for free
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — What argparse does with an invalid value
import argparse\np = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog='demo')\np.add_argument('--mode', choices=['read', 'write'])\n\nprint(p.parse_args(['--mode', 'read']).mode)\np.parse_args(['--mode', 'delete'])   # rejected
read\nusage: demo [-h] [--mode {read,write}]\ndemo: error: argument --mode: invalid choice: 'delete' (choose from 'read', 'write')
actual output, captured from Python 3.11
  • The valid value parses normally.
  • The invalid one never reaches your code — argparse prints the message above and exits with status 2.
  • Note the message lists the permitted values, so the user is told how to fix it. Validating by hand inside your function almost never produces a message that good.
🎯 EXAM TIP
choices= restricts the allowed values and argparse rejects anything else with a clear message before your code runs. Keep it distinct from type=, which converts the string — the two are often used together: type=int, choices=[1, 2, 3].

📘 subprocess: running external commands

The modern call: result = subprocess.run(["git", "status"], capture_output=True, text=True) — pass the command as a LIST (no shell injection), capture stdout/stderr as text, then read result.stdout and result.returncode (0 = success). Add check=True to raise CalledProcessError on failure instead of silently continuing.

Avoid shell=True unless you truly need shell features — with untrusted input it is a command-injection hole. Set timeout= for commands that might hang. subprocess is how Python orchestrates everything else on the machine: git, ffmpeg, database dumps, other scripts.

Exercise form: pass environment variables to a child — subprocess.run(["printenv", "X"], env=dict(os.environ, X="hello"), capture_output=True, text=True) — copy the parent environment and add your variable; the child sees X=hello.

📘 Logging done right

Replace print with logging in anything that runs unattended: logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s"), then per-module logger = logging.getLogger(__name__).

Levels and their meaning: DEBUG (diagnostic detail), INFO (normal operation), WARNING (surprising but handled), ERROR (operation failed), CRITICAL (program cannot continue). Production default is INFO; flip to DEBUG when investigating. Log exceptions with logger.exception("failed to sync") inside an except block — it includes the traceback automatically. Why not print? Logging gives you levels, timestamps, destinations (file, console, aggregator), and an off switch — print gives you none of that.

Exercise details: rotation — RotatingFileHandler("app.log", maxBytes=1_000_000, backupCount=3) rolls at 1 MB keeping 3 backups. And prefer lazy %-style placeholders — logger.info("user %s logged in", name) — the string is only built if the level is enabled, unlike f-strings which always pay.

📘 Scheduling: cron, Airflow, and friends

cron is the Unix scheduler: a crontab line like 0 7 * * * python /home/me/report.py runs daily at 7:00 — the five fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. Windows uses Task Scheduler for the same job.

When jobs have DEPENDENCIES (load → transform → report), plain cron gets brittle — that is what Airflow is for: pipelines defined as DAGs (directed acyclic graphs) of tasks with retries, backfills, and a UI showing exactly what ran and what failed. Ladder of complexity: a loop with time.sleep → cron → Airflow/Prefect/Dagster. Use the lowest rung that meets the need.

Exercise forms: GitHub Actions schedule — in the workflow YAML: on: schedule: - cron: "0 7 * * *"; add workflow_dispatch: to allow manual runs from the UI. In-process scheduling — APScheduler: sched.add_job(job, "interval", minutes=5). And to prevent two simultaneous runs of the same script, acquire a file lock (the filelock library): with FileLock("job.lock"):.

📊 FIGURE — what a scheduler promises
🎯 EXAM TIP
\"At-least-once\" means the job may run more than once on retries or failures, so it must be safe to run twice. That is not a detail of the scheduler — it is a design constraint on your job: write upserts rather than inserts, key each run so a repeat overwrites rather than appends, and never assume a task body executes exactly once.

📘 API authentication: headers, tokens, keys

The most common scheme is a bearer token in a header: headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + token} passed to each request (or set once on a Session). Some APIs use an API key header (X-API-Key) or a key as a query parameter — read the docs, the header name matters.

Never hardcode secrets. Load them from environment variables — os.environ["API_KEY"] — with a .env file (python-dotenv) for local development, and keep .env in .gitignore. A 401 response means your credentials are missing/wrong; 403 means authenticated but not allowed. OAuth flows exist for user-on-behalf access — for service-to-service scripts, tokens and keys cover most of real life.

Exercise patterns: hardcoded keys get committed to git history forever — that is the core danger. The refresh skeleton: make the call, and if r.status_code == 401: token = refresh_token(); retry once with the new token. Secrets from the OS credential store — keyring.get_password("service", "user"). And send keys over HTTPS only — HTTP transmits them in plaintext.

Exact exercise form: password = keyring.get_password("my_service", "my_user") — the OS credential store, never the source code.

📘 Pagination and rate limits

APIs return big collections in PAGES. Two styles: page/offset (?page=2 or ?offset=100&limit=50) and cursor-based (the response includes next_cursor or a next URL — follow it until absent). The loop: request, extend results, read the next marker, repeat while it exists.

Rate limits say how many requests per window you may make; a 429 Too Many Requests means slow down — read the Retry-After header if present and sleep that long. The robust client pattern: retry on 429/5xx with exponential backoff (sleep 1s, 2s, 4s… plus jitter), give up after N attempts, and log what happened. Being polite is also being reliable.

Exercise forms: be polite in loops — time.sleep(1) between calls. Exponential delays 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 — time.sleep(2 ** attempt). Declarative retry — tenacity: @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(5), wait=wait_exponential()). Session-level automation — mount urllib3’s Retry on an HTTPAdapter so 429/5xx retry transparently. Flattening pages — all_items.extend(page["items"]) in the pagination loop.

Exact exercise forms: respect rate limits — time.sleep(1) inside the loop; auto-retry 5xx/429 — build a urllib3 Retry, wrap in HTTPAdapter, session.mount("https://", adapter); flatten pages — while url: data = get(url); all_items.extend(data["items"]); url = data.get("next").

📘 Building a tiny API client

Wrap an API in a small class so the rest of your code never touches HTTP: the constructor stores a requests.Session with base URL and auth headers; one private _request(method, path, **kw) does the actual call, raise_for_status, backoff-retry, and JSON parsing; public methods read like the domain — client.get_user(42), client.list_orders(status="open").

Benefits: auth and retries live in ONE place, tests can mock the client instead of the network, and switching providers touches one file. Add __repr__ that hides the token, and raise your own exception type so callers catch ApiError — not requests internals.

Exercise shape: class APIClient: def __init__(self, base_url, token): self.session = requests.Session(); self.session.headers.update({"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}). Then endpoints read like the domain: def get_user(self, user_id): return self._request("GET", f"/users/{user_id}"); a WeatherClient adds def get_weather(self, city): the same way. Worth the class whenever you make many related calls needing shared auth, retries, and error handling.

📊 FIGURE — typing an API boundary
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Declaring the model
from pydantic import BaseModel\n\nclass User(BaseModel):\n    id: int\n    name: str
  • The annotations are not documentation — Pydantic enforces them when the object is constructed, so a missing field or a wrong type raises a ValidationError at the boundary rather than a confusing failure deep in your code.
  • Used as a FastAPI response model it also generates the OpenAPI schema, so the docs and the validation cannot drift apart.
  • This is the difference that matters against TypedDict: that one is a hint for the type-checker with no runtime effect; this one actually rejects bad data.

Written from the Pydantic API rather than executed — pydantic is not installed in the environment these notes were checked in.

🎯 EXAM TIP

📘 Merging, joining, reshaping

merge is SQL join: pd.merge(orders, customers, on="customer_id", how="left") — how = inner (matches only), left (keep all left), outer (keep all). Check row counts before and after: an unexpected explosion means duplicate keys (a many-to-many you did not intend). concat stacks DataFrames vertically.

Reshaping: pivot_table(index="region", columns="month", values="sales", aggfunc="sum") goes long→wide; melt goes wide→long (the tidy shape most tools want). Long/tidy for computation and plotting libraries, wide for human-readable tables — knowing which shape a tool wants is half of pandas fluency.

Exercise calls: different key names — pd.merge(df1, df2, left_on="user_id", right_on="id"). Stack vertically — pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True). Promote a column to the index — df = df.set_index("id"). Quick two-way counts — pd.crosstab(df.gender, df.country).

📊 FIGURE — drop_duplicates and its arguments
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — De-duplicating on one column
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['email'])\n\n# keep the most recent record per email instead\ndf = df.sort_values('updated_at').drop_duplicates(subset=['email'], keep='last')
  • subset= chooses which columns define \"duplicate\". Without it, two rows count as duplicates only if every column matches — which is rarely what you mean for a customer table.
  • keep='first' is the default, so the row that survives is whichever came first in the current row order. If that matters, sort before dropping — as the second line does.
  • keep=False removes all copies, which answers a different question: \"show me only the emails that appear exactly once\".

Written from the pandas API rather than executed — pandas is not installed in the environment these notes were checked in.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming drop_duplicates(subset=['email']) keeps the newest record. It keeps the first in current row order, which is arbitrary unless you sorted. Sort first, then drop with keep='last'.

📘 Type hints, the useful core

Annotations document intent and let tools catch bugs before running: def total(prices: list[float], tax: float = 0.0) -> float:. Modern syntax (3.10+): int | None for optionals, plain list[str] and dict[str, int] — no typing imports needed for the basics.

Hints are NOT enforced at runtime — they power your editor’s autocomplete and a checker like mypy or pyright, which reads them and flags mismatches (passing a str where list[float] is expected) statically. Start pragmatic: annotate public function signatures and dataclasses; skip obvious locals. @dataclass plus hints replaces hand-written __init__ boilerplate beautifully.

Exercise forms: a lookup that can miss — def find_user(user_id: int) -> User | None: — the | None says callers must handle absence. The escape hatch Any (from typing) means anything goes — use it sparingly, because every Any is a place the checker goes blind.

📊 FIGURE — typing a dict with fixed keys
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — It types the dict without changing it
from typing import TypedDict\n\nclass Point(TypedDict):\n    x: int\n    y: int\n\npt: Point = {\"x\": 3, \"y\": 4}\nprint(pt)\nprint(isinstance(pt, dict))\nprint({k: v.__name__ for k, v in Point.__annotations__.items()})\nprint({\"x\": \"not an int\", \"y\": 4})   # no error at run time
{'x': 3, 'y': 4}\nTrue\n{'x': 'int', 'y': 'int'}\n{'x': 'not an int', 'y': 4}
actual output, captured from Python 3.11
  • The value is a plain dict — isinstance(pt, dict) prints True. Nothing new exists at run time.
  • The annotations are recorded, which is what lets mypy and your editor autocomplete the keys and flag a typo.
  • The last line is the limit: a string where an int was declared runs happily. TypedDict is checked by the type-checker, never by Python.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Reach for TypedDict when the data stays inside your own program and you want the keys known — it is cleaner than dict[str, Any] and costs nothing at run time. Reach for Pydantic when the data arrives from outside and actually needs validating.

\n

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

\n
THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
\n
THE 3-STEP LOOP
\n\n\n\n
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
\n
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
\n\n\n\n\n
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
\nStart the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
\n
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
\n
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
\n
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers \"learn it in 25 minutes\" instead of hours.
\n
